title: Accountability and Professional Conduct

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Accountability is best understood as a name attached to a piece of work. When you sign an assessment, a medication entry, or a note, you are stating: if someone asks why this happened, I am the person who answers. Two things follow from that. First, you cannot hand the answer to someone else — 'the charge nurse told me to' may explain a decision, but it does not move your name off the chart. Second, it covers what you did not do. A check you were supposed to make and forgot is still yours to answer for, which is why accountability is always stated as actions and omissions rather than actions alone.

### Question 2

It helps to sort the rules a nurse works under by who wrote them and what each one can take away. The profession wrote the Code of Ethics; violating it damages your standing among peers. The employer wrote the policy manual; violating it can cost you that job. The accreditor's standards apply to the organization, not to you personally. The state legislature wrote the Nurse Practice Act, and that is the only one of the four that is actual law — which is why the board of nursing, and no one else, can end your ability to practice anywhere in that state. When a question asks what governs 'scope of practice,' it is asking which of these carries legal force.

### Question 3

Two separate documents are doing two separate jobs here, and confusing them is the usual source of error. The medical record is the patient's story: what was given, what was observed, what was done next. It must be complete and factual because the next clinician makes decisions from it. The occurrence report is a message to the organization's safety and risk staff: here is what happened and what conditions allowed it. Its usefulness is statistical — if fifteen reports name the same infusion pump, the pump is the problem, and no amount of counseling individual nurses would ever have revealed that.

### Question 4

Picture three drivers who each end up with the same dented fender. One meant to press the brake and pressed the accelerator for an instant — an honest slip, so you steady that driver rather than punish them, and then ask why two pedals that do opposite things sit an inch apart. One had fallen into the habit of rolling through a particular stop sign because it had always been clear before; that person is not being defiant, they have stopped seeing the hazard, so what changes their behavior is someone explaining why it is real. One was racing another car at double the limit; they already knew and proceeded anyway. The dent is identical in all three cases, which is the whole point — the damage tells you nothing about which driver you are dealing with. Whether an error reaches the patient is often chance, so the behavior is what must be judged.

### Question 5

There are two distinct jobs inside any delegation, and only one of them is handed over. The doing is handed over: the assistant walks the patient. The deciding and the watching are not. Someone had to judge that this patient was stable enough to walk, that this assistant had been checked off on the skill, and that the result would be followed up on. If it later emerges that the assistant had never been trained, 'they were the one walking the patient' does not answer the question of who decided they could. That is where the phrase nursing students hear constantly comes from: you can delegate the task, but you cannot delegate the accountability.

### Question 6

Think of these as two different doors that can close. Losing a job closes one door: that employer, that building, that paycheck. Losing or restricting a license closes all of them at once, because the license is what makes a person employable as a nurse anywhere in the state. Different parties control the two doors — a manager and a human resources department control the first, a state agency controls the second — so one does not automatically swing the other. A nurse can be terminated without the board ever hearing about it, and a nurse can be reported to the board by a patient, a pharmacist, or a colleague while the employer takes no action at all.

### Question 7

Imagine a city asking residents to report potholes, but fining every caller fifty dollars for the trouble. The calls stop, the potholes remain, and the city's data now shows a road with no problems at all. Change one thing — every caller receives a message a week later saying the hole was filled — and the reports pour in. Near misses are potholes nobody has hit yet, and they are the cheapest information a hospital will ever get, because the cost of learning has been paid by luck instead of by a patient. Anything that makes reporting expensive in time, embarrassment, or risk does not reduce the hazards; it only reduces your view of them.

### Question 8

The instinct is to treat asking for help as an admission of weakness, and it is worth seeing why that instinct runs backwards. Saying 'I have not done this and I need someone with me' accomplishes two things simultaneously: the patient gets a competent pair of hands, and you get the supervised repetition that makes you competent for next time. Simply refusing the assignment would accomplish only the first. The piece students most often miss is that an assignment does not transfer the outcome upward. The charge nurse may have made a poor assignment, and that is a real and separate problem — but the hands on the patient and the signature in the chart are still yours.

### Question 9

Order matters more here than students expect. The first move after an error is not confession and not paperwork — it is going to the patient, because the drug is already in them and the clinical question of what it may do is now live. The prescriber comes next, since that is the person who can order monitoring, labs, or a reversal agent. Documentation follows, and it must be honest about what was given, because the next nurse and the next provider will make decisions from it. Notice what 'no harm yet' does and does not change: it changes none of the steps. A drug that reached the wrong patient is an error that happened, not a near miss that was caught.

### Question 10

The category is usually settled by what the person believed at the moment they acted. 'I did not mean to do that' points to human error. 'I always do it this way and nothing has ever gone wrong' points to at-risk behavior — the person is not being defiant, they have simply stopped seeing the hazard, often because the shortcut saves time and has never yet cost anything. 'I was told plainly this was dangerous and I did it anyway' points to reckless behavior. The middle category is the one most often misclassified, and the tell is a sincere belief that the shortcut is fine. Once someone has been told directly and continues, that belief is no longer available as an explanation.

### Question 11

The clarifying comparison is the coworker who is visibly impaired and about to drive. Nobody seriously argues for taking notes and seeing whether it happens again next week, because the danger is not next week — it is in the next ten minutes. A nurse caring for patients while impaired is in exactly that position, except the risk falls on people who cannot see it coming and cannot decline the ride. The part that makes reporting feel like betrayal is also worth examining: in many states a report routes the colleague into a confidential monitoring and treatment program rather than straight to losing a license. Saying nothing leaves them alone with the problem until something happens that no program can undo.

### Question 12

A useful way to test this claim is to ask what an outside enforcer can actually detect. It can detect a falsified record, an expired license, a diverted narcotic. It cannot detect that you skipped reading a safety update on a drug you give daily, or that you estimated a blood pressure because you were running behind, or that you noticed your own assessments getting thinner over a difficult month. If fear of being caught were the only motivation in play, everything undetectable would quietly erode — and a great deal of nursing is undetectable. That is the practical reason professions govern themselves from the inside: external rules only ever reach the bottom of the behavior, never the top.
